feedback: If a learner picks an adaptation without a reason: ask which challenge it solves (darkness, pressure, or scarce food).
If a learner thinks deep animals would simply be crushed: explain that soft, water-filled bodies with no trapped air spaces do not collapse under pressure the way a gas-filled body would.

If a learner names cold as the single biggest problem: agree the deep sea is cold, but redirect to crushing pressure as the dominant hazard they are underestimating, and note that hydrothermal vents are actually scalding hot.
activities.intendedInsight: Each deep-sea feature is a response to a specific environmental challenge; soft bodies with no air spaces survive pressure. The deep is genuinely cold, but crushing pressure is the dominant, commonly-overlooked hazard — while vents themselves are hot.
learnerActions: List the three main challenges of the deep: total darkness, crushing pressure from kilometres of water, and scarce food.

For a deep-sea creature, choose adaptations and justify each against a challenge: e.g. huge eyes OR a light organ for darkness; a soft, water-filled body with no air spaces for pressure; a big mouth and slow metabolism for scarce food.
If an equip-and-test builder is available, select a light organ / eye type / body type / mouth, then test whether the creature survives, and revise choices that fail.
Explain why a soft, water-filled body with no air spaces resists crushing pressure, rather than being crushed as a gas-filled surface fish would be.

Rank the hazards: the deep sea is both cold and under crushing pressure, but note that crushing pressure is the dominant and most-underestimated challenge — and that hydrothermal vents are actually hot, not freezing.
activities.title: Adaptation to challenge: equip a creature for the deep
